q: On a notice board every line of text is small and grey except one word set very large in bright red. Which principle is most directly at work in making that word the first thing noticed?

opts.t: Emphasis through contrast of size and colour
Rhythm through repetition of equal units

why: One element is made to differ strongly from its surroundings in size and colour, which creates a focal point. Rhythm and symmetry depend on repetition or mirroring, not on one standout item.

q: A wedding invitation has identical floral borders and centred text, so its left half is a mirror image of its right half. What type of balance does it use?
why: Equal visual weight mirrored about a central axis is symmetrical balance. Asymmetrical balance uses unlike elements of equal visual weight.

q: A large dark rectangle sits on the left of a poster, close to the edge. To balance the layout without mirroring it, which addition on the right works best?

opts.t: A large pale shape placed right next to the dark rectangle on the left
A tiny faint dot placed very close to the centre line
A small, bright, high-contrast shape placed far toward the right edge
Nothing, because an asymmetrical layout can never be balanced

why: Visual weight works like a lever: a light but striking element far from the centre can offset a heavy one, using weight and distance together. A faint dot near the centre adds almost no counterweight.

q: In a form, each label sits just above its input box, with a larger gap before the next label-box pair. Users read each label and box as one unit. Which Gestalt law explains this?
why: Elements that are close together are perceived as belonging together. The grouping here comes from the gaps, not from matching colour or shape.

q: A grid of evenly spaced dots has alternate columns coloured red and blue, and viewers see vertical stripes. Which law is mainly responsible?
why: Items that share colour are grouped. Because the spacing is even, proximity cannot be what creates the stripes.

q: A logo shows a circle drawn with several gaps in its outline, yet viewers read it as a complete circle. Which law is at work?
why: The mind fills in missing parts to perceive a whole, familiar shape.

q: In a well-known type of ambiguous image, viewers can see either a white vase or two dark faces in profile, but not both at the same moment. Which concept does this illustrate?
why: The same boundary can be read as an object (figure) or as the background (ground), and perception flips between them.

q: Two lines cross to form an X, and viewers perceive two smooth lines passing through the crossing rather than two V shapes touching at a point. Which law explains this?
why: The eye prefers to follow smooth, uninterrupted paths rather than abrupt changes of direction.

q: On a building facade, tall narrow windows alternate with short wide windows across the whole width, creating a visual beat. This is an example of:
why: Two unit types repeating in turn give an alternating rhythm. Regular repetition of one unit would be simple rhythm.

q: Which pair of lengths is closest to the golden ratio (about 1.618 to 1)?
why: 8 divided by 5 is 1.6, the closest of these. 3:2 is 1.5, 4:3 is about 1.33 and 2:1 is 2.

q: A magazine page uses a very large headline, a medium subheading and small body text. What is the main purpose of these size differences?

opts.t: To fill the page area evenly
To make every line equally prominent
To signal order of importance and guide the reading sequence
To reduce the number of colours needed

why: Hierarchy ranks information so the reader knows what to read first. Equal prominence would remove that order.

q: Which line treatment would most naturally convey calm and stability in a poster for a meditation retreat?

opts.t: Thick lines crossing at steep angles

why: Horizontals suggest rest and stability, like a horizon. Sharp diagonals and zig-zags suggest tension and movement.

q: A flat circle is given a gradient from light to dark on one side and a soft shadow beneath, so that it now looks like a ball. In design terms the element has moved from:

opts.t: a two-dimensional shape to an implied three-dimensional form

why: Shape is flat and defined by its outline. Shading and cast shadow add the illusion of volume, which makes it a form.

q: A photograph of rough tree bark is printed on smooth glossy paper. What kind of texture does the image convey?

opts.t: No texture, because the surface is flat

why: The eye reads roughness, but the finger feels only smooth paper. That is implied texture, as opposed to actual texture.

q: In a logo, the white gap between two black shapes is arranged so that it forms an arrow. This clever use of the empty area is called:
why: The empty area around and between shapes can carry meaning of its own; here it forms a hidden arrow.

q: A brochure uses one typeface family, a fixed palette of three colours and the same margins on every page, so the pages feel like they belong together. Which principle does this describe?
why: Consistent type, colour and spacing make separate parts read as one whole.

q: A web page is dominated by blue panels, blue text and blue icons. The designer wants the 'Apply' button to stand out most. Which choice is most effective?

opts.t: Make it a saturated orange, the complement of blue, with clear space around it
Make it a slightly different blue, the same size as other items
Add a thin blue border and keep it among the other buttons
Make it a pale tint of blue so it looks gentle

why: Emphasis needs strong difference. A complementary hue plus isolation (space) sets it apart from the surrounding blues, whereas similar blues blend in.

q: Six icons are identical in colour and equally spaced. Three are enclosed in one rounded box and three in another box. Viewers see two groups. Which Gestalt principle best explains this?
why: Items sharing a bounded area are grouped. Spacing and colour are equal, so proximity and similarity cannot explain the grouping.

q: In some traditional art, the most important figure is drawn much larger than the others, regardless of real size. Which idea is being used?

opts.t: Hierarchical scale, where size signals importance

why: Scale is deliberately exaggerated to rank figures by importance rather than to show realistic proportion.

q: A decorative badge has elements spreading outward evenly from a single central point, like spokes of a wheel. What type of balance is this?
why: Elements arranged around a common centre give radial balance.

q: A banner shows a row of circles whose diameter shrinks by the same step from left to right. This progressive change is best called:
why: A gradual, ordered change in size, colour or direction is gradation; it leads the eye along the row and suggests depth or movement.

q: A page repeats the same shape, size, colour and spacing everywhere, and viewers find it monotonous. What would best relieve this?

opts.t: Repeating the same elements even more often
Introducing variety through changes in scale, colour or shape

why: Too much sameness is dull; controlled variety adds interest while unity keeps the page coherent.

q: On the traditional artist's (RYB) colour wheel, which set contains only primary colours?
why: Red, yellow and blue are the RYB primaries. Red, green and blue are primaries of the additive RGB model, not of the artist's wheel.

q: On the RYB wheel, mixing equal parts of red and blue gives which secondary colour?
why: Red + blue = violet, yellow + blue = green, red + yellow = orange.

q: On a 12-hue RYB wheel, which of these is a tertiary colour?
why: A tertiary is a primary mixed with a neighbouring secondary; blue-green comes from blue and green. Violet and orange are secondaries, yellow is a primary.

q: Wheel order around the circle: yellow, yellow-orange, orange, red-orange, red, red-violet, violet, blue-violet, blue, blue-green, green, yellow-green. Which hue is directly opposite yellow-orange?
why: Yellow-orange is 6 steps from blue-violet, half-way round the 12-hue wheel.

q: Wheel order around the circle: yellow, yellow-orange, orange, red-orange, red, red-violet, violet, blue-violet, blue, blue-green, green, yellow-green. Which three hues form an analogous scheme centred on blue?
why: Analogous colours are three neighbours on the wheel. Violet and green are two steps away from blue, not adjacent.

q: Wheel order around the circle: yellow, yellow-orange, orange, red-orange, red, red-violet, violet, blue-violet, blue, blue-green, green, yellow-green. Which pair completes a triadic scheme with orange?
why: A triad uses hues four steps apart. From orange, four steps lead to violet and eight steps lead to green.

q: Wheel order around the circle: yellow, yellow-orange, orange, red-orange, red, red-violet, violet, blue-violet, blue, blue-green, green, yellow-green. A designer chooses red as the base of a split-complementary scheme. Which pair accompanies it?
why: Red's complement is green. Split-complementary uses the two hues either side of that complement: blue-green and yellow-green. Red-orange and red-violet would make an analogous scheme.

q: Beams of red light and green light of full strength overlap on a white screen in a dark room. What colour appears where they overlap?
why: Light mixes additively: red + green = yellow. Adding blue as well would give white.

q: Why do CMYK printers add a separate black ink instead of relying only on cyan, magenta and yellow?

opts.t: Black is the only ink that can mix with white paper
Overlapping the three inks usually gives a muddy dark brown, not a true black
Cyan, magenta and yellow cannot produce any dark colours
Black is needed so that additive mixing can take place

why: Real inks are impure, so C+M+Y gives a murky dark tone and uses much ink. A separate key (black) plate gives crisp text and deep shadows. Print mixing is subtractive, not additive.

q: Adding white to pure red gives pink. In colour terminology, pink here is a:
why: Tint = hue plus white, shade = hue plus black, tone = hue plus grey.

q: A designer mixes a pure green with a mid grey to soften it. The resulting colour is called a:
why: Adding grey lowers saturation and gives a tone; white would give a tint and black a shade.

q: In an interior mock-up, which wall colour would tend to make the wall look nearer to the viewer, as warm colours do?
why: Warm, saturated hues tend to advance, while cool, pale hues tend to recede.

q: A start-up selling organic vegetables wants a primary brand colour that most directly suggests nature and freshness. Which is the best choice?
why: Green is widely associated with plants, growth and freshness, so it supports the message of organic produce.

q: A global brand finds that white packaging suggests mourning in some markets and purity in others. What does this show?

opts.t: White has one fixed universal meaning
Colour associations depend only on wavelength
Colour meanings are learned and vary across cultures, so research is needed
Colour psychology is irrelevant to packaging

why: Associations come from culture and context, not from light itself, so designers must check local meanings.

q: Which text and background pairing gives the best legibility for body text?
why: Legibility depends mainly on strong lightness (value) contrast. The other pairings have weak lightness differences.

q: A dashboard uses only red and green dots to mark loss and profit, and some viewers with red-green colour blindness cannot tell them apart. Which fix is best?

opts.t: Add redundant cues such as symbols, labels or clear lightness differences
Use pale pink and pale mint instead
Make the dots smaller so they look neater

why: Information should not depend on hue alone. Shape, text or a strong lightness difference works for everyone; saturation or paler tints do not solve the confusion.

q: A coloured poster is photocopied in black and white. Which property of its colours decides whether its elements still stand apart from each other?
why: Greyscale keeps only lightness. Two different hues of equal value can turn into the same grey and merge.

q: In paint, mixing two complementary colours in roughly equal amounts, such as red and green, tends to produce:
why: Complements absorb much of each other's light in subtractive mixing, so the result is a muted neutral.

q: A doorway must let almost every adult walk through without ducking. Which stature value should set its minimum clear height?

opts.t: A high percentile, such as the 95th or 99th, of the user population

why: Clearances are set for large users, because anyone smaller then fits as well. Using the average would leave about half the users ducking.

q: A wall-mounted emergency switch must be reachable by nearly everyone standing. Which user group should set the maximum mounting height?

opts.t: Tall users, around the 95th percentile of reach
The eye height of tall users
Small users, around the 5th percentile of reach

why: Reach limits are set for small users: if they can reach it, taller users can too. Designing for tall reach would leave small users unable to use it.

q: Why is designing for the 'average person' often a poor strategy?

opts.t: Very few people are close to average on every body dimension at once
Averages cannot be calculated for body data
Average dimensions are always the largest

why: A person average in height may be above or below average in arm length or hand size, so a design built on averages fits few people well.

q: In Norman's terms, an affordance is:

opts.t: A label that tells users where to press
A relationship between an object and a user that allows an action, such as a handle allowing grasping
A sound or light shown after an action
A restriction that stops wrong actions

why: Affordance is what an object makes possible. Telling users where to act is a signifier, response after action is feedback, and blocking wrong actions is a constraint.

q: A door has a flat plate with the word PUSH printed on it. The printed word is best described as a:
why: A signifier is a perceivable cue that shows where or how an action should happen.

q: On a four-burner hob, the knobs are laid out in the same 2 x 2 pattern as the burners they control. Which principle does this show?
why: Mapping is the relationship between controls and their effects; matching the spatial layout makes it obvious which knob controls which burner.

q: After a user presses a lift call button, the button lights up and a soft chime sounds. Which principle is this?
why: Feedback tells the user that the action was registered.

q: A SIM card tray is shaped with one corner cut off so that the card fits only one way round. This is an example of:

opts.t: A physical constraint that prevents error

why: Shape that blocks the wrong orientation is a physical constraint, a basic way of error-proofing.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven principles of universal design?
why: The seven principles are equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use.

q: Replacing round door knobs with lever handles helps people with weak grip or full hands. Which universal design principle is mainly served?

opts.t: Size and space for approach and use

why: A lever can be operated with a push of the forearm and needs little grip strength, so the effort is low.

q: According to Hick's law, what happens as the number of equally likely choices in a menu increases?

opts.t: Decision time rises, though not in direct proportion

why: More options mean longer decision time, growing roughly with the logarithm of the number of choices. Grouping options reduces the choices seen at once.

q: According to Fitts' law, which target is fastest to select with a pointer or thumb?

opts.t: A small target close to the starting position
A large target close to the starting position
A large target far from the starting position
A small target far from the starting position

why: Movement time grows with distance and shrinks with target size, so large and near is quickest and small and far is slowest.

q: A phone number is printed as 98765 43210 rather than as ten unbroken digits. Which idea best explains why this helps?

opts.t: Hick's law reduces the number of choices
Chunking reduces the load on working memory
Figure-ground separates digits from the page

why: People hold a limited number of items in working memory; grouping digits into chunks makes the string easier to read and remember.

q: A file upload screen shows a progress bar and the message 'Uploading, 60 percent'. Which of Nielsen's heuristics does this best satisfy?

opts.t: Match between system and the real world

why: The system keeps the user informed about what is happening, within a reasonable time.

q: A menu lists all available commands instead of asking users to type command names from memory. Which heuristic does this follow?
why: Showing options reduces memory load; users only have to recognise the command they want.

q: Which body dimension chiefly determines a comfortable seat height for a chair?

opts.t: Popliteal height (underside of the knee to the floor)

why: A seat close to popliteal height lets the feet rest flat without pressure under the thighs. Sitting elbow height relates to desk or table height.

q: A writing desk is being designed. To keep the forearms roughly horizontal while writing, desk height should be set by the seat height plus which seated dimension?

opts.t: Sitting elbow height above the seat

why: The desktop should sit near elbow level when seated, so the working height is the seat height plus the sitting elbow height. The other dimensions do not set that vertical level.

q: A user holds a new gadget and cannot work out which control will do what they want. Norman would call this a problem in bridging the:
why: The gulf of execution is the gap between what the user wants to do and the actions the device allows. The gulf of evaluation is the difficulty in interpreting the result.

q: Which feature defines a serif typeface?

opts.t: Small finishing strokes at the ends of the main letter strokes
Letters drawn with a single uniform stroke width
Letters joined together in a flowing script
Letters built only from straight geometric blocks

why: Serifs are the small strokes added at the ends of the main strokes of a letter. Typefaces without them are called sans serif.

q: In typography, what does kerning mean?

opts.t: Changing the thickness of every letter
Adjusting the space between a specific pair of letters
Setting the gap between two lines of text
Choosing the width of the page margin

why: Kerning adjusts the space between particular letter pairs (such as A and V) so the spacing looks even. Line spacing is called leading.

q: Text is set at 10 pt with 12 pt leading. A designer adds 3 pt to the leading and leaves the type size unchanged. The new leading is what percentage of the type size?
why: New leading is 12 + 3 = 15 pt. Compared with a 10 pt type size, 15/10 = 150%.

q: Under the road-sign convention followed in India, which shape is generally used for signs that give a mandatory order or a prohibition?
why: Mandatory and prohibitory signs are circular. Warning signs are triangular and informatory signs are generally rectangular.

q: Why is the STOP sign given a unique octagonal shape?

opts.t: So it can be recognised even when its text is hidden or cannot be read
Because octagons are cheaper to cut than circles
Because eight sides stand for eight directions of travel
Because red can only be printed on eight-sided shapes

why: A distinctive silhouette lets drivers identify the sign quickly, even from behind or when the lettering is obscured.

q: What is a pictogram?

opts.t: A letter style used only for headings
A simplified picture that conveys a meaning without relying on words
A table of numbers placed on a poster
A frame that surrounds a logo

why: Pictograms communicate an idea, such as a toilet or a telephone, through a simplified image that crosses language barriers.

q: What is wayfinding in design?

opts.t: A method of printing maps on fabric
A measure of how quickly a road can be built
A system of signs, colours and layouts that helps people find their way in a place
A survey of land carried out before construction

why: Wayfinding covers signage, colour coding, maps and spatial cues that guide people through airports, hospitals, campuses and cities.

q: In India, which certification mark guarantees the quality grade and purity of agricultural produce such as pulses, spices and edible oils?
why: Agmark is the grade-standard mark for agricultural commodities. The BIS Hallmark relates to precious-metal purity and the FSSAI logo to food-safety licensing.

q: A hallmark stamped on a gold ornament in India primarily assures the buyer that:

opts.t: Its gold purity has been tested and certified by a standards body
The ornament was made entirely by hand
The design is protected by copyright
The ornament was made in one particular village

why: A hallmark is a certification of metal purity (fineness) carried out under a standards scheme.

q: The widely used universal recycling symbol is based on which idea?

opts.t: Arrows that chase one another in a continuous loop
A single downward arrow dropping into a box
A leaf placed inside a circle

why: Arrows that follow each other in a loop express the continuing cycle of reusing materials.

q: Which layer is called the primary package of a product?

opts.t: The outer carton used for shipping many units together
The shelf stand that displays the product in a shop
The layer in direct contact with the product, such as a sachet or bottle
The label printed on a delivery truck

why: Primary packaging touches the product directly. Secondary packaging groups units and tertiary packaging is for transport.

q: What is a wordmark in logo design?

opts.t: A logo with only a symbol and no letters
A logo that is a purely abstract shape
A logo formed from a cartoon character
A logo made only of the brand name set in distinctive lettering

why: A wordmark relies on the name itself, treated typographically, to carry the identity.

q: Why do brands often create a mascot?

opts.t: To give the brand a friendly, memorable personality people can connect with
To replace the legal name of the company
To lower the cost of manufacturing
To avoid using colour in advertising

why: A character humanises a brand, is easy to remember and can work across advertising, packaging and social media.

q: In typography, legibility mainly refers to:

opts.t: How well page layout keeps readers engaged across many pages
How easily individual characters can be told apart and recognised
The number of typefaces used in one document
How attractive a page looks at first glance

why: Legibility is about the clarity of letterforms. Readability is the broader comfort of reading text, shaped by size, spacing and layout.

q: Which setting is generally hardest to read in a long paragraph?

opts.t: Dark text on a light background
Text set entirely in capital letters

why: Capitals share a uniform height, so words lose their distinctive shapes and reading slows down.

q: A logo must stay recognisable both as a tiny app icon and on a large hoarding. Which quality of a good logo is this?
why: A scalable logo keeps its clarity at very small and very large sizes, so it is built from simple, bold shapes.

q: Why are large letters, strong contrast and simple typefaces preferred on highway signs?

opts.t: Drivers must read the message quickly from a distance while moving
Ornamental typefaces are not allowed to be painted
Signs are meant to be admired as decorative art
Small letters are illegal on public roads

why: Signage is judged by how fast and how accurately a moving viewer can read it, which favours size, contrast and simplicity.

q: The ISI mark on a household product in India signifies that the product:

opts.t: Conforms to an Indian standard for quality and safety

why: The ISI mark, issued under the Bureau of Indian Standards, indicates conformity with the relevant Indian standard.

q: The Arts and Crafts movement, led in Britain by William Morris, stood for:

opts.t: Embracing factory mass production without change
Abstract art with no practical use
Reviving skilled handcraft and honest materials in response to industrial goods
Using plastic as the main material of everyday objects

why: Morris and his followers criticised poorly made machine goods and promoted well-crafted, beautiful, useful objects.

q: Who founded the Bauhaus school in Weimar in 1919?
why: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus, which aimed to unite art, craft and industrial technology.

q: Which idea best sums up the Bauhaus approach to design?

opts.t: Bring art, craft and technology together, with form shaped by function
Cover every surface with rich ornament
Return to the guild system of the Middle Ages
Treat design as purely personal expression

why: The Bauhaus taught a unified education in art, craft and technology and favoured simple forms suited to mass production.

q: Which description fits Art Deco design of the 1920s and 1930s?

opts.t: Flowing plant-like curves in muted colours
Bold geometric forms, zigzags and luxurious materials that express glamour

why: Art Deco is known for symmetry, streamlined geometry and rich decorative materials.

q: The Memphis Group, formed in Milan in 1981 around Ettore Sottsass, is known for:

opts.t: Playful, brightly coloured furniture with bold patterns and unusual shapes

why: Memphis broke with austere modernism using colourful laminates, loud patterns and irreverent forms.

q: Which set of qualities is typical of Scandinavian design?

opts.t: Heavy carved ornament and dark stains
Simple, functional forms in light woods that serve everyday comfort

why: Scandinavian design values simplicity, usefulness, natural materials and democratic access to good design.

q: Why is the Eames India Report of 1958 important in Indian design education?

opts.t: It recommended setting up a national design institute, which led to NID
It banned the import of furniture
It created the first road-sign standard
It founded the Indian Institutes of Technology

why: Charles and Ray Eames, invited by the Government of India, recommended a design institute; this led to the National Institute of Design.

q: The Eames India Report led to the establishment of the National Institute of Design. In which city and decade was NID founded?
why: The report was written in 1958 and NID was founded in Ahmedabad in 1961, which is the 1960s.

q: Charles and Ray Eames are best known for:

opts.t: Moulded plywood and fibreglass furniture and films about design

why: The Eameses are famous for their moulded plywood and plastic chairs, and for exhibitions and films.

q: Which designer, long associated with the company Braun, is known for the motto 'less, but better'?
why: Dieter Rams set out ten principles for good design built on restraint, honesty and usefulness.

q: Which architect, the last director of the Bauhaus, is linked with the maxim 'less is more'?
why: Mies van der Rohe directed the Bauhaus until its closure in 1933 and championed 'less is more'. Gropius was the founder, Sullivan the 'form follows function' voice, and Venturi opposed minimalism.

q: The phrase 'form follows function' is associated with which American architect?
why: Louis Sullivan used the phrase for tall office buildings, and it later became a principle of modern design.

q: Which style of about 1890 to 1910 is marked by sinuous, organic lines inspired by plants and flowers?
why: Art Nouveau used flowing whiplash curves and natural motifs in architecture, glass, posters and furniture.

q: Which Dutch movement used straight lines, right angles and primary colours, as in the paintings of Piet Mondrian?
why: De Stijl reduced art and design to horizontal and vertical lines and red, yellow, blue with black, white and grey.

q: Which Swiss-French architect designed the Capitol Complex of Chandigarh?
why: Le Corbusier designed the Capitol Complex and the major government buildings of Chandigarh.

q: The American architect Louis Kahn designed the campus of which institution in Ahmedabad?
why: Louis Kahn designed the brick campus of IIM Ahmedabad, working with Indian architects such as Balkrishna Doshi.

q: Robert Venturi's remark 'less is a bore' was a challenge to which idea?

opts.t: The Arts and Crafts revival of handcraft
The modernist austerity summed up as 'less is more'

why: Venturi, a leading postmodern architect, answered Mies van der Rohe's 'less is more' by arguing for richness, ornament and complexity.

q: Victor Papanek's book 'Design for the Real World' argued that designers should:

opts.t: Take social and environmental responsibility for their work

why: Papanek criticised wasteful, manipulative design and urged designers to serve real human needs.

q: Which Bauhaus-trained designer pioneered tubular-steel furniture such as the Wassily chair?
why: Marcel Breuer applied bent tubular steel to chairs in the 1920s, taking inspiration from bicycle handlebars.

q: Raymond Loewy became famous in 20th-century industrial design for popularising:

opts.t: Streamlined styling of products such as vehicles and appliances

why: Loewy applied smooth, aerodynamic-looking styling to locomotives, cars, appliances and packaging to make them more appealing.

q: Tiny knots are tied on cloth with thread before dyeing, leaving dotted patterns. Which craft is this, traditional in Gujarat and Rajasthan?
why: Bandhani is a tie-dye craft in which fabric is plucked and bound into tiny knots that resist the dye.

q: In which technique are yarns tied and dyed in patterns before weaving, giving softly blurred motifs, as in Pochampally?
why: Ikat is a resist-dyeing method applied to the yarns before they are woven, producing characteristic feathery edges.

q: Which silk sari of Patan in Gujarat is a double ikat, with both warp and weft yarns resist-dyed before weaving?
why: Patola is a double-ikat textile where both sets of threads are dyed to a plan and must align exactly when woven.

q: Which craft uses a pen or block to draw or print on cotton with natural dyes, often showing epic scenes, in places such as Srikalahasti in Andhra Pradesh?
why: Kalamkari means pen work. Srikalahasti kalamkari is freehand drawn with a kalam, and Machilipatnam kalamkari is block printed.

q: Which delicate, mostly white thread embroidery on fine cotton or muslin is associated with Lucknow?
why: Chikankari is Lucknow's shadow-like white-on-white hand embroidery with many named stitches.

q: Which embroidery of Punjab uses floss silk darning stitches in floral patterns on coarse cotton shawls and dupattas?
why: Phulkari means flower work. Dense silk thread stitched from the back of the cloth creates bright floral and geometric designs.

q: Which heavy embroidery, with gold or silver metallic thread, sequins and stones, flourished in Mughal courts?
why: Zardozi (zar means gold, dozi means sewing) is rich metal-thread embroidery used on royal costumes and furnishings.

q: A blackened zinc-based alloy with designs inlaid in silver is the hallmark of which metalwork from Bidar in Karnataka?
why: Bidri ware is cast from an alloy chiefly of zinc, inlaid with silver, and darkened with a special soil. This gives its striking contrast.

q: Tribal artisans in Bastar, Odisha and West Bengal make figures by covering a wax model with clay, melting the wax out and pouring in molten metal. Which craft is this?
why: Dhokra is non-ferrous metal casting using the lost-wax (cire perdue) process, in which each mould is used once.

q: Brightly lacquered wooden toys and dolls turned on a lathe are associated with a town in which state?
why: Channapatna, near Bengaluru in Karnataka, is called the toy town for its lacquered wooden toys.

q: Lightweight toys carved from soft wood and painted with vegetable and enamel colours come from a village near Vijayawada. Which craft is this?
why: Kondapalli toys of Andhra Pradesh are carved from a light wood known as tella poniki and depict village life and mythological scenes.

q: Which Jaipur craft uses quartz powder instead of clay and a glaze coloured with cobalt blue?
why: Jaipur blue pottery is made from a quartz-based dough, shaped, painted and glaze-fired, and is not made of regular clay.

q: Which folk painting of the Mithila region of Bihar is noted for fine line work, bold colours and filled borders?
why: Madhubani (Mithila) painting traditionally decorated the walls of homes with mythological and nature motifs.

q: Which tribal art of Maharashtra uses white rice-paste pigment on mud walls, with circles, triangles and squares forming human figures?
why: Warli painting depicts daily life, harvests and rituals through simple geometric shapes in white on a red-brown earthen wall.

q: Which Odisha craft consists of mythological narratives painted on prepared cloth, with Puri as a major centre?
why: Pattachitra (patta means cloth) uses stiffened cloth, natural mineral colours and bold outlines to tell stories of Jagannath and Krishna.

q: Which fine wool from the Changthangi goat of Ladakh, hand-spun and woven in Kashmir, makes soft shawls?
why: Pashmina is the fine undercoat wool of the Changthangi goat, spun and woven by hand in Kashmir.

q: Bagru in Rajasthan is known for dabu printing. What kind of technique is this?
why: In dabu a paste of mud, lime and gum is block-printed to resist the dye, so the covered parts stay undyed.

q: What does a Geographical Indication (GI) tag on a craft or product signify?

opts.t: The product is made by a government agency
The product is sold at a lower price
The product uses only eco-friendly packaging
The product's quality or reputation is linked to a specific place of origin

why: A GI tag recognises goods such as Darjeeling tea or a regional craft whose qualities come from their place of origin.

q: Rani ki Vav at Patan in Gujarat is a famous example of which kind of structure?
why: A step-well is a well reached by flights of steps down to the water, often richly carved. Rani ki Vav is a celebrated Gujarat example.

q: In Indian architecture, what is a jali?

opts.t: A perforated screen of stone or lattice that admits light and air while giving privacy

why: A jali is a pierced screen, often geometric, that filters light, lets in air and screens people from view.

q: A jharokha, common in Rajasthani and Mughal buildings, is:

opts.t: A projecting, enclosed balcony with a window on an upper floor

why: A jharokha is an overhanging balcony on an upper storey, from which one can look out onto the street or court.

q: Which classical form of Kerala combines dance and drama, with elaborate painted faces and towering headgear?
why: Kathakali is a dance-drama of Kerala known for its colour-coded face makeup, large costumes and expressive eye and hand gestures.

q: Which description fits Thanjavur painting of Tamil Nadu?

opts.t: Gold foil, raised gesso work and semi-precious stones, usually around a central deity
White rice paste on mud walls
Black line work filling double-lined borders
Natural-dye drawing of epics on cotton using a pen

why: Thanjavur paintings are made in a rich style with gesso relief, gold leaf and inlaid stones, and the main figure sits in the centre.

q: Which craft of Bengal layers old saris and joins them with running stitches to make quilts and wraps?
why: Kantha uses simple running stitches to hold layers of worn cloth together and decorates them with embroidered motifs.

q: A company needs to make several lakh identical plastic bottle caps with fine threads at low cost per piece. Which process is most suitable?
why: Molten plastic is forced into a steel mould, giving fast, repeatable, detailed parts, so the high tooling cost is spread over many pieces.

q: Which process is normally used to make hollow, thin-walled plastic bottles such as those for edible oil?
why: A heated plastic tube (parison) is inflated with air against a mould wall, producing a hollow container.

q: A heated thermoplastic sheet is pulled over a mould by suction to make shallow packaging trays. This process is called:
why: Vacuum forming draws a softened sheet onto a mould, ideal for shallow trays and blister packs.

q: Which product is best made by extrusion, where material is pushed through a shaped die?

opts.t: A bottle with a handle and neck
A long plastic pipe of constant cross-section

why: Extrusion produces continuous lengths with a fixed profile, such as pipes, rods and window frames.

q: Letterpress printing belongs to which family of printing?
why: In relief printing the inked surface stands above the non-printing areas, as in letterpress type and flexography.

q: In gravure (intaglio-type) printing, the ink is held in:

opts.t: Water-attracting areas of a flat plate
Open mesh areas of a fabric screen
Tiny engraved recesses on the cylinder or plate

why: Gravure and intaglio carry ink in recessed cells or lines, and pressure transfers it to paper; this suits long runs and fine tonal images.

q: Offset lithography works on the principle that:

opts.t: Oil-based ink and water repel each other, and the inked image is transferred through a rubber blanket
Ink is pushed through a fine mesh onto the surface
Raised metal type presses ink directly onto paper
Ink is held in deep engraved grooves

why: The plate is flat; image areas accept ink and wet areas reject it. The image is offset to a blanket before reaching the paper.

q: Which printing method is the most practical for printing a bold design directly on a cotton T-shirt?
why: Ink is squeezed through a stencilled mesh, so it can print on fabric, plastic, glass and curved objects.

q: Flexography is widely used for printing on packaging films and corrugated board mainly because it uses:

opts.t: Flexible rubber or photopolymer relief plates and fast-drying inks

why: Flexible relief plates can print on non-absorbent and uneven surfaces at high speed, ideal for packaging.

q: If an A4 sheet is folded in half across its longer side, the resulting size is:
why: In the A series each size is half the area of the one before it, so half of A4 is A5.

q: In the paper trade, the term GSM stands for:
why: GSM states the mass of one square metre of paper; a higher GSM means a thicker, heavier sheet.

q: Bamboo is considered a good design material for furniture and baskets chiefly because it is:

opts.t: Fast-growing, light and strong in tension along its fibres

why: Bamboo is a grass that matures in a few years and has strong longitudinal fibres, so it is renewable and strong for its weight.

q: What distinguishes a thermoplastic such as polypropylene from a thermoset such as phenolic resin?

opts.t: A thermoset can be melted and remoulded repeatedly
A thermoplastic can never be recycled
A thermoplastic is made only from natural fibres
A thermoplastic softens again when reheated and can be remoulded

why: Thermoplastics soften on heating and harden on cooling repeatedly; thermosets undergo permanent chemical cross-linking when cured.

q: A dovetail joint is most commonly used at the corners of:
why: Interlocking wedge-shaped pins and tails resist being pulled apart, which suits drawer fronts and boxes.

q: Molten aluminium is forced under high pressure into a steel mould to produce thousands of identical small parts with a smooth finish. This is:
why: Pressure die casting gives accurate, smooth parts in high volume; sand casting is better for large or few pieces.

q: Why is a spanner often made by forging rather than by casting?

opts.t: Forging aligns the grain flow of the metal, giving higher strength and toughness
Forging avoids the use of metal

why: Compressive shaping of heated metal refines and aligns its grain, improving strength and resistance to impact and fatigue.

q: A lathe is mainly used to produce:

opts.t: Round (cylindrical) parts by rotating the workpiece against a cutting tool
Prints by pressing ink on paper

why: The workpiece spins while a tool removes material, giving shafts, legs of furniture and bowls.

q: In fused deposition 3D printing, an object is created by:

opts.t: Stretching a heated sheet over a form
Depositing melted filament layer by layer
Pouring molten metal into a sand mould
Cutting it from a solid block with a saw

why: This is an additive process: material is added in layers, unlike subtractive machining that removes material.

q: Which element added to steel gives stainless steel its resistance to rusting?
why: Chromium forms a thin, self-healing oxide layer on the surface that protects the iron beneath.

q: When toughened (tempered) glass breaks, it:

opts.t: Crumbles into small blunt granules, reducing the risk of deep cuts
Splits into a few long sharp shards

why: Rapid heating and cooling puts the surface in compression, so on failure it fragments into small, relatively safe pieces.

q: Tanning of animal hides is carried out to:

opts.t: Make the hide stable, durable and resistant to rotting

why: Tanning chemically stabilises the collagen fibres, so leather does not putrefy and stays supple and strong.

q: A designer is choosing material for the handle of a cooking pan that must not become too hot to hold. Which property matters most, and which material fits?

opts.t: Low thermal conductivity; phenolic resin or wood

why: A handle should be a heat insulator. Aluminium and copper conduct heat well; phenolic resin and wood do not.

q: Raw natural rubber is sticky and softens in heat. Heating it with sulphur improves its elasticity and durability. This process is named:
why: Sulphur forms cross-links between rubber polymer chains, giving a tougher, elastic material suited to tyres.

q: Timber is seasoned before making furniture mainly to:

opts.t: Add moisture so it bends easily
Reduce its moisture content so it warps and cracks less afterwards

why: Unseasoned wood shrinks and distorts as it dries; seasoning brings it close to the moisture level of its place of use.

q: In waste management the three Rs stand for:
why: The 3Rs are a hierarchy for cutting waste, with reduction being the most effective step.

q: Turning discarded scooter inner tubes into stylish wallets is an example of:
why: Upcycling converts waste into products of higher value or quality than the original item.

q: Compared with a linear "take, make, dispose" economy, a circular economy aims to:

opts.t: Keep materials and products in use as long as possible and design out waste
Increase the volume of products discarded
Make products that last for one use

why: Circular thinking designs for reuse, repair and recycling so that materials loop back instead of becoming waste.

q: The cradle-to-cradle design idea holds that:

opts.t: Materials should be designed as nutrients that cycle in biological or technical loops
Only recycled paper should be used
Every product should be buried after use

why: Cradle-to-cradle treats waste as a resource: biological nutrients return safely to nature, technical ones to industry.

q: A life-cycle assessment of a product examines its environmental impact:

opts.t: From raw material extraction through manufacture, use and disposal
Only after it is thrown away

why: Looking at every stage prevents shifting the burden from one stage to another.

q: A carry bag is labelled compostable and another biodegradable. Why is "compostable" the more reliable claim?

opts.t: It must break down into non-toxic compost within a defined time under composting conditions
It is made only of metal
It needs no standard or test

why: "Biodegradable" has no time limit and can leave residues; compostable products are tested to break down fully in a set period.

q: Which is the best way to dispose of an old mobile phone?

opts.t: Give it to an authorised e-waste recycler

why: Phones contain recoverable metals and also toxic substances, so they need proper treatment.

q: The main purpose of the Paris Agreement of 2015 is to:

opts.t: Limit global warming by cutting greenhouse gas emissions through national commitments

why: Countries agreed to keep the rise in global average temperature well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.

q: The Kyoto Protocol is best described as an international treaty that:

opts.t: Fixed the price of crude oil
Set binding emission-reduction targets for developed countries

why: Adopted in 1997, it committed industrialised countries to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

q: A product's carbon footprint refers to:

opts.t: The area of land it occupies
The total greenhouse gas emissions linked to its life cycle
The number of colours used on it

why: It expresses emissions in carbon dioxide equivalent for a product or activity.

q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
why: Wind, like sunlight and flowing water, is naturally replenished, whereas fossil fuels are finite.

q: To make a product easier to recycle at end of life, a designer should prefer:

opts.t: Welded plastic shells with no access
Screws and snap-fits that let different materials be separated

why: Easy separation allows each material to be sorted and recycled instead of becoming mixed waste.

q: Biodiversity means:

opts.t: The number of factories in a region
The variety of living organisms in an area or on Earth

why: Biodiversity covers variety among species, within species and in ecosystems.

q: Rainwater harvesting helps water conservation by:

opts.t: Collecting and storing rain or recharging groundwater
Draining rain quickly into the sea

why: Capturing rain reduces dependence on piped or ground supplies and helps recharge aquifers.

q: What is the central idea of the passage?

passage: A good chair is rarely noticed. Its designer's achievement is the absence of complaint: no ache in the lower back after an hour, no wobble when someone leans to reach a cup, no edge pressing against the thigh. It is a reminder that restraint takes skill, because every decision that the user never has to think about was once a decision the designer had to make, often after many failed prototypes.

q: What can be inferred about Meera from the passage?

opts.t: She had long wished to learn pottery.
She had recently been living in a state of rush and tension.
She disliked the potter and avoided his lane.
She was herself a skilled potter.

passage: Meera had walked past the potter's lane every morning for six years without once going in. That Tuesday the rain drove her under his tin awning, and she watched him centre a lump of wet clay on the wheel. His hands barely moved. Meera laughed, surprised at herself. For the first time in months, the hurry she carried like a bag of stones felt a little lighter.

q: The author's main point is that

opts.t: technical knowledge enriches a designer so long as it does not limit imagination.
designers should leave coding to specialists.
potters make better designers than programmers.
a designer's tools should decide what is imagined.

why: The author rejects the idea that learning code ends one's identity as a designer, but warns against letting tools limit imagination.
passage: Some say that a designer who learns to code ceases to be a designer. This confuses the tool with the thinking. A potter who studies glazes is not a chemist, yet no one claims her pots suffer. Such knowledge is simply another kind of material sense. Knowing how a material behaves, whether clay, timber or software, lets a designer propose what is possible rather than merely what is pretty. The real danger lies elsewhere: in letting the limits of one's tools quietly decide what one imagines. Fluency should widen the designer's questions, not narrow them.

q: What does the idiom 'back to the drawing board' mean?

opts.t: to start planning afresh after an attempt has failed
to return to the studio to relax
to finish the final drawing neatly
to ask a senior for approval

why: The idiom comes from design and engineering: after a plan fails, one begins again with a new design.

q: In a certain code, CAT is written as ECV. How is DOG written in that code?
why: Each letter is shifted two places forward: C+2=E, A+2=C, T+2=V. So D+2=F, O+2=Q, G+2=I giving FQI.

q: If PAINT is written as QBJOU, how is COLOR written?
why: Each letter moves one place forward: C-D, O-P, L-M, O-P, R-S, giving DPMPS.

q: In a code, each letter is replaced by its mirror in the alphabet (A with Z, B with Y, and so on). How is DESK written?
why: Mirror of a letter at position n is at 27-n. D(4)->23=W, E(5)->22=V, S(19)->8=H, K(11)->16=P: WVHP.

q: Ravi walks 5 km north, turns right and walks 4 km, then turns right again and walks 5 km. How far is he from the starting point, and in which direction?
why: North 5 km, then east 4 km (right turn from north), then south 5 km (right turn from east). North and south cancel; he is 4 km east of the start.

q: In the early morning Neha stands so that her shadow falls on her right-hand side. Which direction is she facing?
why: The morning sun is in the east, so shadows fall west. If west is on her right, she faces south (facing south, right is west).

q: In a row of 31 students Tara is 12th from the left and Uma is 9th from the right. How many students stand between them?
why: Uma's position from the left is 31-9+1=23. Students between positions 12 and 23 are 23-12-1=10.

q: A is taller than B, B is taller than C, D is taller than A, and E is shorter than C. Who is the third tallest?
why: The order from tallest is D > A > B > C > E, so the third tallest is B.

q: Five people stand in a queue. Anil is ahead of Bela, Bela is ahead of Chitra, Dev is directly behind Chitra, and Esha is ahead of Anil. Who is in the middle of the queue?
why: Order from the front: Esha, Anil, Bela, Chitra, Dev. The third of five is Bela.

q: Pointing to a man, a woman said, 'He is the son of my mother's only daughter.' How is the man related to the woman?
why: My mother's only daughter is the woman herself, so the man is her son.

q: A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. How is A related to D?
why: A and B are children of C, and C is D's child. So A is D's grandchild, and as a sister she is a granddaughter.

q: Priya's mother is the sister of Arun. How is Arun related to Priya?
why: Arun is her mother's brother, which makes him her maternal uncle.

q: Find the next letter: B, D, G, K, P, ?
why: Positions are 2, 4, 7, 11, 16: differences 2, 3, 4, 5, so next difference is 6 and 16+6=22 which is V.

q: Find the next number: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
why: Differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12 and 30+12=42.

q: Find the next number: 5, 10, 8, 16, 14, 28, ?
why: The rule alternates double and subtract 2: 5x2=10, 10-2=8, 8x2=16, 16-2=14, 14x2=28, so 28-2=26.

q: Find the next pair: AZ, BY, CX, DW, ?
why: The first letter moves forward one place and the second backward one place: D->E and W->V, giving EV.

q: Select the odd one out: 8, 27, 64, 100, 125.
why: 8, 27, 64 and 125 are cubes of 2, 3, 4 and 5. 100 is not a perfect cube.

q: Select the odd one out: pencil, charcoal, crayon, eraser.
why: Pencil, charcoal and crayon are used to make marks; an eraser removes them.

q: Knife : Cut :: Needle : ?
why: A knife is used to cut; a needle is used to sew. The relation is tool to function.
64 is 4 cubed (4x4x4), so 5 cubed is 125.

q: Statements: All designers are observers. Some observers are poets. Conclusions: I. Some designers are poets. II. Some poets are observers. Which follows?
why: 'Some observers are poets' converts to 'some poets are observers', so II follows. The poets among observers need not be designers, so I does not follow.

q: Statements: All circles are shapes. No shape is a line. Conclusions: I. No circle is a line. II. Some lines are circles. Which follows?
why: Circles lie inside shapes and no shape is a line, so no circle is a line (I). II directly contradicts I.

q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 3:30?
why: Hour hand: 3x30+30x0.5=105 degrees. Minute hand: 30x6=180 degrees. Difference is 75 degrees.

q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 7:20?
why: Hour hand: 7x30+20x0.5=220 degrees. Minute hand: 20x6=120 degrees. Difference is 100 degrees, which is under 180.

q: If 5 March 2025 was a Wednesday, which day was 5 April 2025?
why: March has 31 days, so 5 April is 31 days later. 31 mod 7 = 3, and Wednesday + 3 days = Saturday.

q: Today is Thursday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from today?
why: 100 = 14x7 + 2, so the day is two days after Thursday, which is Saturday.

q: In the late afternoon, a man stands facing his own shadow. In which direction is he facing?
why: In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so shadows fall east. Facing his shadow, he faces east.

q: A school replaced desks with standing desks and found that class test scores rose 6 per cent over the term. The principal concludes that standing desks improve learning. Which assumption does the conclusion most depend on?

q: Neighbourhoods with more street cafes record less petty crime. A councillor proposes subsidising cafes to cut crime. What is the main flaw in the reasoning?

How can we make the app better for everyone?

why: It names a specific group, a specific behaviour and observable data, so it can be investigated; the others are vague or too broad.

q: A furniture brand publishes a report headlined 'Study shows our chairs are rated best'. The brand paid for the study, and participants were recruited from its showrooms. What is the most serious problem with the findings?

opts.t: Chairs cannot be rated by users.
The study was too short to measure comfort.
The sample was drawn from the brand's own customers, so it is likely to favour the brand.

why: Recruiting from showrooms builds in selection bias, reinforced by the funder's interest; neither fact shows the chairs are better than rivals.

q: A brief for a child's water bottle reads: 'Make it beautiful, modern, loved by everyone, very cheap yet with a premium feel.' What is the main weakness of the brief?

opts.t: Its goals are vague and partly conflicting, and it sets no measurable constraints.

why: 'Beautiful' and 'modern' cannot be tested, and 'very cheap' conflicts with 'premium'. A good brief gives usable limits such as cost, size and material.

q: A designer must choose between plastic and steel for a school-bag buckle. Plastic is cheaper and lighter but cracks with use; steel lasts much longer but costs more and is heavier. Which statement correctly describes the trade-off?

opts.t: Steel is better on every measure.
Plastic is better on every measure.
Lower cost and weight are gained at the expense of durability, and vice versa.
Cost and durability are unrelated here.

why: Each material wins on some measures and loses on others: plastic on cost and weight, steel on durability.

q: After a mural was painted at a bus stop, footfall rose 30 per cent, but sales in nearby shops did not change. Which conclusion is best supported?

opts.t: More people passed the stop, but this did not by itself raise shop sales.
The mural caused the rise in footfall and will raise sales later.
Footfall and sales are never connected.

why: The data show higher footfall and flat sales. They do not show that the mural caused the footfall, nor that sales will rise.

q: Argument: Libraries should stay open in the evening because evening users are mostly students with no quiet place to study at home. Which finding would most strengthen this?

opts.t: Libraries in other cities close at six.
Many students visit libraries in the morning.
A survey of evening users finds most have no quiet space at home.

why: The argument rests on evening users lacking quiet space at home; the survey directly supports that premise.

q: A brand claims: 'Our packaging is eco-friendly because it contains 30 per cent recycled paper.' Which assumption does the claim require?

opts.t: Customers will buy anything labelled eco-friendly.
The recycled content makes the packaging environmentally better overall, with no larger offsetting harm.
The packaging was cheap to produce.

why: The claim moves from a feature (recycled paper) to a verdict (eco-friendly). It needs the assumption that other harms do not outweigh the benefit.

q: Students who use the design library more often earn higher grades. A teacher concludes that library use raises grades. Which alternative explanation shows the reasoning may be reversed?

opts.t: Grades are awarded at the end of the year.
Students who are already strong and motivated tend to use the library more.
Some students use the library for printing.

why: If high performers are the ones who visit more, then ability drives library use, not the other way round.

q: A city bans plastic bags. Bag litter in drains falls 40 per cent the next year, and officials credit the ban. Which new fact would most weaken that credit?

opts.t: In the same year the city doubled the frequency of drain cleaning.
The ban was widely reported in the press.

why: Doubled cleaning could by itself explain less litter in the drains, so the fall may not be due to the ban.

q: Which source gives the strongest evidence for the claim 'large-print menus increase orders from older diners'?

opts.t: A restaurant owner's impression after switching menus.
A blog post praising large print.
A design award won by a large-print menu.
An eight-week comparison in which the same restaurants alternated menu types and counted orders by diners over 60.

why: A controlled comparison with counted outcomes isolates the effect of the menu; impressions, praise and awards do not.

q: A survey asks: 'Don't you agree that the ugly new signage should be removed?' What is wrong with the question?

opts.t: It is too short to be understood.
It is a leading, loaded question that pushes respondents towards one answer.
It asks about signage rather than people.

why: The words 'Don't you agree' and 'ugly' suggest the preferred answer, producing biased results.

q: A designer must choose between a dense dashboard showing every metric and a clean one showing five. Which pair of values is in tension?

opts.t: Speed of the server versus screen width.
Completeness of information versus ease of scanning.

why: More metrics give completeness but make the screen harder to scan; fewer metrics do the reverse.

q: Every handmade product at a craft fair was priced above 500 rupees. Ravi bought an item at the fair for 300 rupees. Which statement must be true?

opts.t: Ravi's item was not a handmade product.
Ravi's item was a machine-made product of poor quality.
Ravi got a discount on a handmade item.
The fair had no handmade products.

why: If all handmade items cost more than 500, a 300-rupee item cannot be handmade. Nothing else is guaranteed.

q: A researcher wants to test whether tactile maps help visually impaired travellers find their way. Which design gives the most convincing answer?

opts.t: Participants are asked afterwards whether they liked the map.
Only participants who already own a map are tested.
One expert walks the route and describes it.
The same participants walk comparable routes with and without the map, in alternating order, and time and errors are recorded.

why: A within-participant comparison with alternating order and measured outcomes controls individual differences and order effects.

q: A brief says: 'Design a poster to reduce food waste in the canteen.' Which addition would most improve it?

opts.t: A request to use the brightest colours available.
Who the audience is, where the poster will hang, and a measurable target such as cutting plate waste by 20 per cent in a term.
A note that the poster should be creative.
The name of the head of the canteen.

why: A useful brief defines audience, context and success measures, so that the design can be judged.

q: 'Every successful studio I know has an open-plan office. So open-plan offices make studios successful.' What is the main flaw?

opts.t: It uses a number of studios that is too large.
It assumes that offices have a plan.
It treats a feature common among successes as a cause, without checking unsuccessful studios.
It disagrees with the success of studios.

why: Looking only at successes ignores studios that also have open plans but failed, and it ignores other possible causes.

q: A junction recorded 10 accidents in the year before a new sign was installed and 5 in the year after. The council claims the sign halved accidents. Which additional fact would most weaken this claim?

opts.t: In each of the five years before that, the junction averaged about 5 accidents.
The sign was green in colour.
The junction is near a school.
The council had installed signs elsewhere.

why: If 5 is the usual level, the earlier 10 was an unusual peak and the fall is a return to normal, not an effect of the sign.

q: A city plans to replace 200 bus-stop benches with leaning rails to discourage loitering. Which group's interests does the plan most clearly overlook?

opts.t: Bus drivers who follow fixed routes.
Advertisers who rent the bus-stop panels.
Elderly and disabled passengers who need to sit while waiting.

why: Removing seating directly affects people who cannot stand for long; the other groups are not affected in the same way.

q: Which of these statements is a factual claim that can be checked by measurement?

opts.t: The tiles look warm and welcoming.
The tiles lose 0.5 mm of thickness for every 10,000 footsteps.
The tiles are the best choice for a modern home.
The tiles will make the hall feel larger.

why: Only wear per number of footsteps can be measured and verified; the others are matters of taste or perception.
